bridgeConcepts: English name and German Name provide a visible memory cue.
transferMappings.learnerExplanation: English name can help you remember German Name. Keep the German capital letter and learn the full frame Ich heiße ...
transferMappings.teacherNotes: Treat this only as a surface-form memory cue; do not imply identical pronunciation or complete phrase structure.

positiveExamples.note: Written-form cue; German noun capitalization still applies.

review.notes: Cognate status, pronunciation caveat, and usefulness need competent bilingual review.

bridgeConcepts: English and German use different default capitalization for common nouns.
transferMappings.learnerExplanation: Watch the capital letter: English normally writes common nouns such as coffee in lowercase, while German writes Kaffee with a capital K.
transferMappings.teacherNotes: Present as a written-language contrast, not as a prediction that every English-speaking learner will make this error.

positiveExamples.note: The German noun begins with a capital.

negativeTransferRisks: An English lowercase habit may produce kaffee in German writing; do not generalize this to proper nouns or sentence-initial words.

review.notes: Contrast and non-universal learner framing need competent bilingual review.

transferMappings.learnerExplanation: No English shortcut is shown here. In the cited beginner examples, both German du and Sie translate as you, so the German relationship choice must be learned directly.
transferMappings.teacherNotes: This is an intentional no-bridge record. It must never be promoted into a displayable similarity by the router.
negativeTransferRisks: Do not use English you alone to choose between German du and Sie.
